pos: n. (proper, a Levite of the restoration; Hebrew, the wasting of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Baqbuqyah, from baqbuq, a flask or bottle — a word formed from the gurgling sound a narrow-necked vessel makes. The name is usually read as emptied by Jehovah, or the wasting of the LORD.
biblical_def: He appears three times, always in a company and always with an office. At the settling of Jerusalem: “And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer: and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren” (Nehemiah 11:17). Among the singers set in order: “Also Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches” (Nehemiah 12:9) — antiphonal choirs, answering each other. And among the gatekeepers: “Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates” (Nehemiah 12:25). He is named as the second, never the principal. The restoration ran on men who held the second place, answered the other choir, and kept a door — and the Holy Ghost saw fit to write their names down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Levite of the restoration, second among his brethren in the thanksgiving and a porter at the gates.
webster_full: PORTER, n. A man that has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.
WARD, n. Watch; act of guarding; garrison; the state of being under guard or in custody.
ANTIPHONAL, a. Consisting of responsive singing; sung alternately by two choirs or divisions.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
SUBORDINATE, a. Inferior in order, in nature, in dignity, in power or importance; occupying a lower place.
scriptures: And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer: and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun.
Also Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches.
Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates.
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
corruption_summary: Christian service is evaluated by prominence, so that a man in the second place is assumed to be waiting for the first; Scripture records Bakbukiah as the second, in a watch and at a gate, and preserves his name.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live distortion is a settled assumption that visibility measures value, which turns every subordinate office into a stepping stone and every long-held second place into a failure. Nehemiah 11:17 describes a man whose whole recorded identity is the second among his brethren. Nehemiah 12:9 has him in a watch, singing over against the other choir. Nehemiah 12:25 has him keeping the ward at a threshold. Three verses, three offices, none of them the first, and his name in the word of God in all three.

The psalmist of the sons of Korah — a family of doorkeepers — put the doctrine in a line: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness. The comparison is not between a great office and a small one but between the meanest place in God's house and the best seat anywhere else. A man who has genuinely made that comparison stops calculating his position, and the church that is full of such men is the one that gets rebuilt.

pos: n. (proper, a Kohathite Levite; Hebrew, a snatching away)
etymology: Hebrew Machath, probably a grasping or a snatching away. Two Levites bear it: one in Samuel's ancestral line, and one who is named first among the Levites who arose at Hezekiah's call to cleanse the house of the LORD.
biblical_def: He stands in the pedigree that runs up to Samuel the prophet: “The son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai” (1 Chronicles 6:35). The great scene is Hezekiah's reformation. The king opened the doors of the house of the LORD in the first month of his reign, gathered the Levites and charged them to sanctify themselves and carry out the filthiness from the holy place, and the response is recorded name by name: “Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi” (2 Chronicles 29:12). His name comes first in the list of those who arose. Later, when the tithes came in and had to be handled honestly, he is among those appointed: “Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah” (2 Chronicles 31:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Kohathite Levite in Samuel's line, and one who arose first at Hezekiah's call to cleanse the temple.
webster_full: KOHATHITE, n. A descendant of Kohath the son of Levi; the division of Levites charged with the holiest vessels.
CLEANSE, v.t. To purify; to make clean; to remove filth or foul matter of any kind.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a supervisor; one who has the care of others.
REFORMATION, n. Change from worse to better; amendment of life, manners, or of anything vicious or corrupt.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy.
scriptures: The son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai,

Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah:

And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God.
And said unto them, Hear me, ye Levites, sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place.
corruption_summary: Reformation is imagined as a change of preaching that leaves the practical house untouched; Hezekiah's began with Levites carrying filth out of the holy place, and continued with honest men set over the tithes.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 29 shows what a reformation actually costs in labour. Hezekiah's charge was blunt: Sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place. The doors had been shut, the lamps put out, the incense unoffered. The first act of renewal was manual: named men, Mahath at the head of them, carrying rubbish out of a building. Sixteen days of it before a sacrifice could be offered. Renewal that never reaches the actual state of the house is sentiment, and Scripture measures it by what gets carried out.

The second stage is just as practical and more easily neglected. When the reformation succeeded, the people brought tithes in heaps, and the immediate problem was administration — and 2 Chronicles 31 lists by name the overseers set over the store, Mahath among them, under Cononiah and his brother. Revival produces resources, and resources require accountable men. A movement that will not appoint overseers over its heaps is preparing its own scandal, and the chronicler thought the names of the men who handled the money worth recording.

pos: n. (proper, a Levite musician; Hebrew, the LORD is strong)
etymology: Hebrew Azazyahuw, from azaz, to be strong, and Yah — Jehovah is strong. Three men bear it: a harper when the ark came up, the father of an Ephraimite ruler, and an overseer of the tithes under Hezekiah.
biblical_def: When David brought up the ark with the appointed music, the instruments were divided by name and by part: “And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel” (1 Chronicles 15:21). The verse before assigns others psalteries on Alamoth; this group has harps on the Sheminith — on the eighth, most likely the lower octave — and the stated aim is to excel. A second Azaziah is the father of the ruler of Ephraim in David's administration: “Of the children of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah” (1 Chronicles 27:20). A third is among the overseers appointed over the tithes in Hezekiah's reformation (2 Chronicles 31:13). The name confesses the strength of the LORD, and the men who bore it are found at a harp, in a governor's house, and over a storehouse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Levite appointed with harps on the Sheminith when the ark was brought up, and as the name of two other men.
webster_full: HARP, n. An instrument of music of the stringed kind, of a triangular figure, held upright and struck with the fingers.
SHEMINITH, n. In the titles of Psalms and in Chronicles, a musical term, generally understood as the eighth, or the octave below.
EXCEL, v.i. To surpass; to exceed; to go beyond others in good qualities or laudable deeds.
PSALTERY, n. An instrument of music used by the Hebrews, the form of which is not now known.
SKILL, n. The familiar knowledge of any art or science, united with readiness and dexterity in execution.
scriptures: And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel. on
Of the children of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah: of the half tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah:

And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God.
And Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was for song: he instructed about the song, because he was skilful. was
corruption_summary: Excellence in worship music is suspected as performance, and incompetence tolerated as humility; Chronicles names the players, assigns their instruments and parts, and says plainly that the aim was to excel.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 15 is the most detailed account of musical arrangement in the Bible, and it is deliberate. Some are set with psalteries on Alamoth, others with harps on the Sheminith to excel, and the next verse adds that Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was for song: he instructed about the song, because he was skilful. Parts assigned, ranges specified, an instructor appointed, excellence named as the goal. Any suspicion that skill in the worship of God is worldly has to reckon with a chapter that plans it in this much detail under David's own hand.

The guardrail is in the same chapter and is severe. The first attempt to bring up the ark ended with Uzza struck dead, and David's explanation is that they sought him not after the due order. The Levites then sanctified themselves and bare the ark upon their shoulders with the staves, as Moses commanded. Skill and order are both required, and neither substitutes for the other: God appoints how he is to be worshipped, and within that appointment he calls for the best men doing their best work. Excellence outside the due order is what killed a man beside a cart.

pos: n. (proper, chief of the captains who came to David; Hebrew, burdensome)
etymology: Hebrew Amasay, from amas, to load or carry a burden. The name belongs to a Kohathite Levite in Samuel's line and, most memorably, to the captain on whom the Spirit came at Ziklag.
biblical_def: He appears in the Levitical pedigree twice: “And the sons of Elkanah; Amasai, and Ahimoth” (1 Chronicles 6:25), and “the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai” (1 Chronicles 6:35). The great verse is at Ziklag, where armed men came to David while he was still an outlaw and he met them with a challenge — if ye be come peaceably I will be knit unto you, but if to betray me, the God of our fathers look thereon and rebuke it. The answer is one of the most stirring pledges of allegiance in Scripture: “Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains, and he said, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The last clause is the ground of the whole: not thou art strong but thy God helpeth thee. The Spirit came upon a soldier to give him the words.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the chief of the captains who pledged allegiance to David at Ziklag, and as a Levite in Samuel's line.
webster_full: ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; the duty of fidelity to a king.
CAPTAIN, n. A head or chief officer; the military officer who commands a company.
ZIKLAG, n. A town given to David by Achish king of Gath, where he dwelt while an outlaw from Saul.
CLEAVE, v.i. To stick; to adhere; to hold to; to unite aptly, as by a natural or strong attachment.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; and in Scripture, an oracle of weight.
scriptures: Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains, and he said, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee. Then David received them, and made them captains of the band.
And the sons of Elkanah; Amasai, and Ahimoth.
The son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai,

And David went out to meet them, and answered and said unto them, If ye be come peaceably unto me to help me, mine heart shall be knit unto you: but if ye be come to betray me to mine enemies, seeing there is no wrong in mine hands, the God of our fathers look thereon, and rebuke it. to
corruption_summary: Loyalty is given to leaders for what they can deliver, and withdrawn when they cannot; Amasai pledged himself to a hunted man with no throne, and gave his reason as the help of God rather than the prospects of David.
corruption_paragraphs: The circumstances make the pledge remarkable. David at Ziklag was a fugitive with a band of the distressed, the indebted and the discontented; Saul was still on the throne; there was nothing to gain by joining him and a great deal to lose. David himself was suspicious enough to challenge the newcomers outright. And the Spirit came upon Amasai and gave him words: Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse. Loyalty that costs nothing and expects a return is not what Scripture means by the word; this is a man committing himself to an anointed king who had no kingdom.

The reason he gives keeps the pledge from being mere partisanship: for thy God helpeth thee. His confidence is not in David's ability or fortunes but in David's God, and the peace he pronounces is threefold — to David, to David's helpers, and implicitly to himself in joining them. That is the shape of Christian allegiance too. The church follows a King whose kingdom is not yet visibly established and whose people are frequently a company of the distressed and the indebted, and her confidence is that God helps him.

pos: n. (proper, a Levite of the sons of Korah; Hebrew, the father has gathered)
etymology: Hebrew Ebyacaph, from ab, father, and acaph, to gather — my father has gathered, or has added. He is a descendant of Korah, and his line kept the gates of the tabernacle.
biblical_def: He stands in the Kohathite pedigree: “Elkanah his son, and Ebiasaph his son, and Assir his son” (1 Chronicles 6:23), and again reckoned upward: “The son of Tahath, the son of Assir, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah” (1 Chronicles 6:37). The office of his line is stated plainly: “And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father, the Korahites, were over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle” (1 Chronicles 9:19). Korah was the Levite who rose against Moses and Aaron and went down alive into the pit; and Numbers 26:11 records, in one of the most consequential asides in the Pentateuch, that the children of Korah died not. From that spared line came the doorkeepers of the tabernacle and the sons of Korah whose name stands over eleven psalms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a descendant of Korah, whose house were keepers of the gates of the tabernacle.
webster_full: KORAHITE, n. A descendant of Korah the Levite; a family of doorkeepers and singers in the house of God.
DOORKEEPER, n. One who guards the entrance of a house or apartment; a porter.
REBELLION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes obedience.
MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a composition consisting in praise or celebration of God.
scriptures: Elkanah his son, and Ebiasaph his son, and Assir his son,
The son of Tahath, the son of Assir, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah,

And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father, the Korahites, were over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle: and their fathers, being over the host of the LORD, were keepers of the entry.
Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not.
corruption_summary: A family is assumed to inherit the reputation of its worst member, and Numbers 26:11 stands against it — the children of Korah died not, and their descendants kept God's doors and wrote his psalms.
corruption_paragraphs: Korah's rebellion is the most spectacular judgment in Numbers: the earth opened and swallowed him and his company, and fire consumed the two hundred and fifty. If ever a family name was ruined, that one was. And then, at the end of a genealogy where hardly anyone looks, Moses writes four words that change everything for that house: Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not. The judgment was exact. It fell where it was deserved and stopped where it was not, and Scripture takes the trouble to say so.

What God did with the spared line is the second half. Ebiasaph's descendants became keepers of the gates of the tabernacle — the sons of the man who had grasped at the priesthood were given the doors to guard — and eleven psalms are inscribed to the sons of Korah, including How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts and As the hart panteth after the water brooks. The family that tried to seize the sanctuary was given a place in it by mercy, and its children sang some of the most tender lines in the Psalter.

pos: n. (proper, a Levite; Hebrew, a rolling or a great one)
etymology: Hebrew Galal, from galal, to roll — the verb of Psalm 37:5, Commit thy way unto the LORD, which is literally roll thy way upon him. Two or three Levites bear the name in the registers of the returned.
biblical_def: He appears in the Chronicler's roll of those who dwelt in Jerusalem: “And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph” (1 Chronicles 9:15). A second Galal is given a pedigree in the next verse: “And Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, that dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites” (1 Chronicles 9:16). The same household appears in Nehemiah's parallel list (Nehemiah 11:17). These are the Levites of the singers' families — Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman — whom David had set over the service of song, and whose descendants came back from Babylon and took up the same work in a ruined city. The villages of the Netophathites near Bethlehem were where the singers lived, because a man who must be at the house of God daily has to live within reach of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Levite of the singers' families in the registers of those who returned from Babylon.
webster_full: ROLL, v.t. To turn on an axis; to move by turning; to commit or cast upon another, as a burden.
JEDUTHUN, n. One of the three chief musicians appointed by David over the service of song in the house of the LORD.
NETOPHATHITE, n. An inhabitant of Netophah, a village near Bethlehem where the singers dwelt.
COMMIT, v.t. To give in trust; to put into the hands or power of another; to entrust.
RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place for some continuance of time.
scriptures: And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph;
And Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, the son of Elkanah, that dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites.

And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer: and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun.
Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
corruption_summary: Life is arranged around work and preference, with the house of God fitted into whatever remains; the singers of the restoration lived in villages within reach of the temple because the service required daily presence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The quiet lesson in these registers is about where people chose to live. The Chronicler notes that the singers dwelt in the villages of the Netophathites, near Bethlehem — close enough to be at the house of God for the daily service. Nehemiah 11 is a whole chapter about who would live in Jerusalem, and it records that the people blessed the men that willingly offered themselves to dwell there, because the city was large and the houses were not builded. Where a household settles is a spiritual decision with consequences that outlast it.

The name itself preaches. Galal is to roll, and it is the verb behind Psalm 37:5, Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass — literally, roll thy way upon him. Proverbs uses the same word: roll thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established. A burden is not committed by being thought about; it is rolled off the shoulder onto another, and the man who has genuinely done it walks differently.

pos: n. (proper, a Gershonite Levite; Hebrew, a plan or device)
etymology: Hebrew Zimmah, a plan, a purpose, and in most other places a wicked device — the word Leviticus uses for the gravest sins. As a personal name it stands for purpose without the pejorative sense.
biblical_def: He is placed in the line of Gershom, Levi's eldest son: “Of Gershom; Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son” (1 Chronicles 6:20), and again in the pedigree of Ethan the singer, reckoned upward: “The son of Ethan, the son of Zimmah, the son of Shimei” (1 Chronicles 6:42). His name appears a third time in the roll of Levites who arose at Hezekiah's summons to cleanse the temple, as the father of Joah: among those who came were “of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah” (2 Chronicles 29:12). The Gershonites carried the curtains, the coverings and the hangings of the tabernacle through the wilderness, work as necessary and as unglamorous as the Kohathites' charge over the holy vessels was honoured. The divisions of Levi are set out in Scripture with care, because God assigns particular service to particular families.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Levite of the line of Gershom, and father of Joah in Hezekiah's reformation.
webster_full: GERSHONITE, n. A descendant of Gershon the eldest son of Levi; charged in the wilderness with the curtains and coverings.

TABERNACLE, n. A tent; in Scripture, the movable sanctuary of Israel in the wilderness.
CHARGE, n. That which is committed to the care or management of another; trust; custody.
DIVISION, n. The act of dividing; a part separated from the rest; a portion; a section.
scriptures: Of Gershom; Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son,
The son of Ethan, the son of Zimmah, the son of Shimei,

Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah:

And they shall bear the curtains of the tabernacle, and the tabernacle of the congregation, his covering, and the covering of the badgers' skins that is above upon it, and the hanging for the door of the tabernacle of the congregation,
corruption_summary: Service in the church is treated as a matter of preference and availability, where the Levitical divisions show God assigning particular work to particular houses and holding them to it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle in Zimmah's line is the ordering of service. Numbers 3 and 4 divide Levi into three houses with three charges: Kohath bore the ark and the vessels, Gershon the curtains and coverings and hangings, Merari the boards, bars, pillars and sockets. Nobody chose his own load, and nobody carried another's. Paul's account of the body works the same way — God hath set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him — and the health of a congregation depends on members doing their own work rather than the work they would prefer.

There is a warning attached to the Gershonite charge that the name makes pointed. Zimmah elsewhere means a wicked device, a purpose formed against God, and Kohath's house had already shown in Korah what happens when a Levite decides his assigned service is beneath him. The cure for discontent with a small charge is not a larger one but the recognition that the curtains had to be carried, that God appointed who would carry them, and that centuries later a son of that house rose first when a king called the Levites to sanctify the temple.
roots_summary: Hebrew Zimmah (H2155), a plan or device; zamam (H2161), to purpose; Gereshom (H1648), Gershom; mishmereth (H4931), a charge or watch.

pos: n. (proper, a warrior who came to David; Hebrew, the LORD keeps)
etymology: Hebrew Shemaryah, from shamar, to keep or guard, and Yah — Jehovah has kept. Several men bear it: a Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag, and two of the men who put away strange wives under Ezra.
biblical_def: He is listed among the mighty men — Benjamites of Saul's own tribe, armed with bows and able to use both the right hand and the left — who came to David at Ziklag: “Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite” (1 Chronicles 12:5). Two men of the same name appear at the other end of the history, in the painful register of Ezra 10: “Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah” (Ezra 10:32) and “Azareel, and Shelemiah, Shemariah” (Ezra 10:41), among those who had taken strange wives and separated from them. The name is a confession that God keeps, and it is borne both by a man who left his tribe's king to join God's anointed while it was dangerous, and by men whose repentance was recorded by name for every later generation to read.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Benjamite warrior who came to David at Ziklag, and as the name of men in the register of Ezra 10.
webster_full: KEEP, v.t. To hold; to retain in one's power or possession; to preserve; to guard; to protect.
PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil; to uphold.
AMBIDEXTER, a. Using both hands with equal facility; as, the Benjamites who could sling stones with either hand.
DEFECTION, n. The act of abandoning a person or cause to which one is bound by allegiance or duty.
REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts or proceedings, for preserving and conveying knowledge.
scriptures: Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite,
They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin.
corruption_summary: A man's standing is judged by the company he was born into, where Chronicles records Benjamites of Saul's own kindred leaving him for David, at cost and while the outcome was still doubtful.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 12:2 is careful to name the tribe: these were of Saul's brethren of Benjamin, armed with bows, able to use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows. Shemariah was one of them. Leaving Saul meant leaving kinsmen, security and the visible throne for a hunted man in the wilderness with no guarantee of an outcome. Scripture consistently honours that kind of decision — Ruth leaving Moab, Moses refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter — and it consistently costs something at the time it is made.

The other Shemariahs give the harder encouragement. Their names stand in Ezra 10, the list of men who had married strange wives and put them away — a register of failure made public and permanent. Both kinds of name are in the same Bible, and the same name is on both lists. A man may appear in the record of God's word as one who came at cost to the right side, or as one who sinned and repented at cost, and it is far better to be in the second list than to be absent from both because nothing was ever risked or ever renounced.
roots_summary: Hebrew Shemaryah (H8114), Jehovah has kept; shamar (H8104), to keep or guard; Tsiqlag (H6860), Ziklag; badal (H914), to separate.

“Of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” — what the coming cost them.
“Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah” — the other kind of list.

pos: n. (proper, men of the restoration; Hebrew, liberal or a gift of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Mattenay, from mattan, a gift — liberal, or gift of Jehovah. Three men bear it, two in Ezra's register of those who put away strange wives and one among the priests in Nehemiah.
biblical_def: Two of the name stand in the register of Ezra 10, a chapter that names every man who had taken a strange wife and separated from her: “Of the sons of Hashum; Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei” (Ezra 10:33), and “Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasau” (Ezra 10:37). A third is a priest in the days of Joiakim: “And of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi” (Nehemiah 12:19). The two books are the record of the same generation at two stages: the men whose repentance was written down in Ezra, and the courses of priests serving in an ordered house in Nehemiah. A name meaning gift stands on both lists, and the second could not have existed without the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of two men in the register of Ezra 10 and of a priest in Nehemiah 12.
webster_full: GIFT, n. A present; any thing given or bestowed; an offering or donation.
LIBERAL, a. Generous; bountiful; munificent; not selfish, narrow or contracted in mind.
COURSE, n. Order of succession; particularly, the order in which the priests ministered in the temple by turns.
CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment of a fault; a public avowal of sin or of faith.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a state in which things bear a due relation to each other.
scriptures: Of the sons of Hashum; Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
And of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi;

Now when Ezra had prayed, and when he had confessed, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, there assembled unto him out of Israel a very great congregation of men and women and children: for the people wept very sore.
corruption_summary: Public confession of sin is regarded as needlessly humiliating and best kept private, and Ezra 10 is a whole chapter of names — the biblical precedent for a repentance that is owned openly where the sin was open.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 10 does something no modern institution would do: it names them. Man after man, family after family, the men who had married strange wives are listed in the word of God, and Mattenai is twice among them. The instinct to keep such things private is not wholly wrong — Scripture guards reputations, forbids talebearing, and orders private sin to be dealt with privately, beginning with a word between two. But where the sin was public and the whole congregation was affected, the repentance was public too, and the chapter opens with Ezra weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, with a very great congregation of men, women and children weeping with him.

What came of it is in Nehemiah. The generation whose failures are listed in Ezra 10 is the generation whose priests are listed by course in Nehemiah 12, serving an ordered house with the wall built and the law read. Repentance recorded in one book and service recorded in the next. The order of those two chapters is the pastoral point: God does not restore a people around their sin, and he does restore a people who have dealt with it.

pos: n. (proper, a high priest of the restoration; Hebrew, known)
etymology: Hebrew Yadduwa, from yada, to know — known, or one whom God knows. He is the last high priest named in the Old Testament, and the last name in its priestly succession.
biblical_def: He sets his seal to the covenant with the chiefs of the people: “Meshezabeel, Zadok, Jaddua” (Nehemiah 10:21). He closes the high-priestly line: “And Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua” (Nehemiah 12:11). And he stands at the end of the register: “The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian” (Nehemiah 12:22). With that verse the Old Testament's record of the priesthood stops. Malachi would prophesy, and then four hundred years of silence, and then a priest named Zacharias executing the priest's office before God in the order of his course would be told that his prayer was heard. The last name in the register means known, and the line it closes was waiting for a High Priest after the order of Melchizedek.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the last high priest named in the Old Testament, who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah.
webster_full: HIGH PRIEST, n. The chief priest among the Hebrews, who alone entered the holy of holies, and that once a year.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; a series of persons or things following one another in time or place.
SEAL, v.t. To fasten with a seal; to ratify; to confirm; to settle.
MELCHIZEDEK, n. King of Salem and priest of the most high God, a type of Christ in his priesthood.
SILENCE, n. Absence of sound or noise; stillness; and hence, the cessation of prophecy between the Testaments.
scriptures: And Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua.
The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian.
But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.
corruption_summary: The Old Testament is often read as ending in failure or simply stopping, where its last priestly register closes a line that had been failing for a thousand years and was waiting for a priest who dies no more.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 12:22 is an unremarkable sentence in an unread chapter and it marks the end of something enormous. The line from Aaron is recorded to Jaddua and then stops. Every man in it had one thing in common, which Hebrews states without malice: And they truly were many priests, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death. A priesthood that must be handed on because its holders keep dying is a priesthood that cannot finally save; the register itself is the argument, generation after generation of men who offered and then were buried.

That is precisely why the next verse in Hebrews lands as it does: But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. The Old Testament ends its priestly list with a man whose name means known, and four centuries later the true High Priest appears, of whom it is said that he ever liveth to make intercession for them. The register closing is not a failure of the Old Testament but the completion of its argument: here are all the priests, here is where they all stopped, and here is why another was needed.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yadduwa (H3037), known; yada (H3045), to know; kohen gadol, high priest; Greek aparabatos (G531), unchangeable.
